ovarian_cyst's FIRST ELIMINATING ROW. Read this one carefully before approving — the full picture, and why argues_against is defensible here specifically where it usually is not.
This is the answer to the page's own question, "Can ovarian cysts make it harder to get pregnant?" — "Typically, no." That is explicit distinguishing language, not an absence-from-a-symptom-list inference: the source is directly answering whether this feature characterizes the condition, and directly saying it does not, typically. The sentence continues by naming the two conditions where cyst-related infertility DOES apply — endometriosis and PCOS specifically, because the cyst there is a marker of the underlying condition rather than the ovarian_cyst condition in its own right. That naming is what pushes this over the bar ADR 0001 sets for argues_against: the source is not merely silent on fertility, it explicitly frames difficulty_conceiving as characteristic of two named alternatives rather than of this condition.
The quote is deliberately the opening two sentences only, not the "Sometimes, though..." sentence that follows — that sentence describes the endometriosis/PCOS exception, which is a genuinely different claim (about THOSE conditions, already carrying their own difficulty_ conceiving=yes weak_support rows) rather than a qualifier that weakens this row's claim about ovarian_cyst. This does not contradict difficulty_conceiving's existing weak_support rows for endometriosis and pcos (both already in the grid) — it is the same source, on the same page, distinguishing the SAME feature across THREE conditions consistently: weak support for the two conditions where it is a named risk, and this row's exclusion for the condition (ovarian_cyst on its own) where the source says it typically does not apply. note: Strong because the source lists it UNDER the androgen-excess heading, and high androgen levels are one of the three characteristic features of PCOS. That is characteristic framing, not a bare symptom list. Retires a feature that had no source until the Office on Women's Health was added.

source_quote: Obesity, weight gain, or trouble losing weight.
note: IMPERFECT MAPPING, deliberately weak. The source names obesity, which is a state rather than a change, alongside weight gain, which is a change. Our feature captures change only. Weak support reflects that the row covers part of what the source says, not all of it.

source_quote: vaginal discharge that looks, smells or feels unusual for you
note: Corroborated by the Office on Women's Health ("Vaginal discharge that may smell foul") and by CDC, which lists "a smelly discharge" among the symptoms that warrant prompt care. Three sources, and again a feature no phase 1 condition claims.

source_quote: bleeding between periods or after sex
note: Corroborated by CDC. Weak because this feature now appears under endometriosis, fibroids and PID; it narrows the differential barely at all.

source_quote: heavy or painful periods that are unusual for you
note: The qualifier matters: "unusual for you" makes this a change from the user's own baseline rather than an absolute level. Our feature captures the level only, so the row loses the comparison the source draws. Weak accordingly.

source_quote: Irregular menstrual periods
note: Listed without emphasis. Weak, and note it pulls the same direction as PCOS and perimenopause — irregularity is the least discriminating finding in the entire knowledge base.

source_quote: 1 in 8 women with a history of PID experience difficulties getting pregnant.
note:
A genuinely new cell — none of the existing 9 rows touch fertility. difficulty_conceiving currently supports endometriosis, ovarian_cyst, pcos and sexually_transmitted_infection (batch_09); PID was the one obvious gap given it is literally what an untreated STI becomes.
The number in the quote ("1 in 8") is the source's own wording, quoted verbatim as required — it is not converted into the row's strength. CLAUDE.md's "never invent probabilities" rule governs what WE assert as a strength value, not whether a cited sentence may itself contain a figure; the strength here is weak_support, an ordinary ordinal judgement like every other row, not a reading of "1 in 8" as somehow stronger or weaker than a plain-language claim would be.
Weak, not strong, and deliberately so: this describes a CONSEQUENCE of a past history of PID ("with a history of PID"), not a presenting symptom a user reports during an acute episode — the same category as the STI fertility row already in the grid (batch_09, sexually_transmitted_infection/difficulty_conceiving, also weak, also quoting a "can lead to" / "left untreated" framing). Keeping both weak is consistent: PID and STI are causally linked conditions in this knowledge base, and their evidence rows should not silently imply stronger claims than either source actually makes for the acute presentation.

source_quote: Fever (100.4° F or higher)
note: Named directly among the signs, with a threshold. Strong because none of PCOS, endometriosis or fibroids causes fever, so this feature does almost all its work here — it is the clearest infective signal in the set. The source states the temperature; we do not store it, because our feature is a yes/no and inventing a numeric threshold we cannot ask about would be false precision.

source_quote: PID can come on fast, with extreme pain and fever, especially if it is caused by gonorrhea.
note: Same sentence as the row above, supporting a second cell. NHS gives the other half of the picture — "Your symptoms may start quickly over a few days, or develop slowly and get worse over time" — which is why this is weak: both onsets occur, so sudden onset raises PID a little without gradual onset arguing against it.

source_quote: Promptly see a doctor if you have any genital symptoms such as an unusual sore, a smelly discharge, burning when peeing, or bleeding between periods
note: Weak: "burning when peeing" appears in a list of triggers for seeking care rather than as a characteristic sign, and it is at least as suggestive of a urinary tract infection, which is now its own condition.

source_quote: pain felt deep inside when you have sex
note:
Note the wording — "deep inside" — which matches how the Office on Women's Health distinguishes deep from entrance pain for endometriosis.
WORTH WATCHING: this feature now has rows for endometriosis, fibroids and PID. A feature that supports three of nine conditions separates very little, and its earlier billing as highly discriminating is now clearly wrong. It still earns its place — it raises all three above the rest — but next_question should not expect much from it.

source_quote: PID can come on fast, with extreme pain and fever, especially if it is caused by gonorrhea.
note: Weak because the source qualifies it — "especially if it is caused by gonorrhea" — so extreme pain describes one presentation rather than the condition.

source_quote: A feeling of pressure, discomfort, aching, or fullness in the pelvis
note: Strong: this is precisely THE FINDING this condition was added to explain (see the condition note — abdominal_swelling_or_pressure had no non-mass explanation). Corroborated by the opening summary sentence, not separately quoted here: "The pressure from prolapse can cause a bulge in the vagina that can sometimes be felt or seen."

source_quote: Aging. Pelvic floor disorders are more common in older women. About 37% of women with pelvic floor disorders are 60 to 79 years of age, and about half are 80 or older.
note: Mapped to the single top band (55_plus) rather than split across multiple bands the way adenomyosis's and primary_ovarian_insufficiency's open-threshold age claims were (batches 11, 18) — the source's own figures (60-79, 80+) both already sit entirely within 55_plus, the widest available band, so there is no ambiguity about which bands qualify the way there was for "over 30" or "before 40". Weak: a prevalence statistic about who GETS the condition, not a symptom a source calls characteristic — the same distinction already applied to every other age_band row in this session's batches.

source_quote: Women with pelvic organ prolapse may feel uncomfortable pressure during physical activity or sex.
note: Weak — "uncomfortable pressure," not pain specifically, and the sentence groups sex with physical activity generally rather than calling it out. Consistent with pain_with_sex's position as one of the least discriminating features in the knowledge base (batch_10, batch_14, batch_20).

source_quote: Leaking urine (incontinence) or problems having a bowel movement
note: Only the urinary half of this compound sentence is mapped — "problems having a bowel movement" names a second organ system with no corresponding value in urinary_symptoms' allowed_values ([none, frequency, incontinence, difficulty_passing_urine]), and mapping bowel problems onto a urinary feature would misstate what the source says. Weak: listed among several findings, and this feature already carries rows for fibroids, ovarian_cyst, urinary_tract_infection and perimenopause.

source_quote: Menopause and perimenopause are a natural part of life. This happens when your periods change and eventually stop due to lower hormone levels. It usually affects women between 45 and 55 but it can happen earlier.
note:
THE ROW THIS CONDITION EXISTS FOR. Our 45_to_54 band sits almost exactly on the source's 45-55 range. Strong, and the only strong age row in the knowledge base — for every other condition age is a risk factor, but here it is close to definitional.
Note the qualifier "but it can happen earlier": age does not rule perimenopause out, which is why there is no argues_against row for the younger bands.

source_quote: Perimenopause ends when you reach menopause. Menopause is when you have not had a period for 12 months.
note:
Absent periods ARE menopause by the source's own definition — a stronger statement than a symptom listing, which is why this is strong support.
CORRECTED at review: the quote first drafted here was transcribed from the page as read in a browser, not from the fetched document, and did not appear in the corpus. `make verify-quotes` caught it. The claim is unchanged; the citation is now real.

source_quote: During perimenopause, your periods may become irregular, lighter or heavier.
note: The source names irregularity as what perimenopause does to periods, which is what makes it strong rather than merely listed. Note it pulls the same direction as PCOS and PID — irregularity remains the least discriminating finding in the knowledge base, and age is what separates these three.

source_quote: Trouble sleeping, such as trouble falling asleep or getting back to sleep when you wake up. Over time, a lack of sleep can lead to fatigue and memory problems.
note: Weak, and the mapping is indirect: the source describes fatigue as a consequence of disturbed sleep rather than a symptom in its own right. Included because it retires an orphan feature and because tiredness in a woman over 45 genuinely belongs in this differential — but a reviewer could reasonably reject it as too many steps from the text.

source_quote: You may have mood swings, low mood or depression.
note: Corroborated by MedlinePlus ("Mood changes, which can make you feel moody, anxious, or more irritable"). Weak: non-specific, and it appears under PCOS and endometriosis too. Retires an orphan feature.

source_quote: You may get more UTIs (urinary tract infections) or symptoms that feel like a UTI. This includes feeling pain or a burning sensation when you pee and needing to pee more often than usual, including at night.
note: The source's own framing matters here: this is not "perimenopause causes pain when urinating" as an independent symptom, it is "perimenopause makes UTIs more likely, and can also mimic UTI symptoms without an actual infection" — see urinary_tract_infection's own causes list in nhs/urinary_tract_infection.json, which separately names "having been through the menopause" as a UTI risk factor. Two conditions genuinely overlapping for a stated physiological reason (falling oestrogen thins the urinary tract lining, named explicitly on this page under "Vaginal problems"), not a coincidence in the source material. Kept weak accordingly — the row raises perimenopause a little without claiming this symptom points there over an actual UTI.

source_quote: You may get symptoms such as dryness, a burning feeling, irritation or itching in and around the vagina. These symptoms can also make sex feel painful.
note: Same sentence, second cell — "these symptoms can also make sex feel painful" refers back to the vaginal dryness/irritation just named. Weak, same reasoning as vulval_itching above: this feature already supports endometriosis, fibroids, PID, STI and thrush (see batch_10 and batch_12 on it becoming one of the least discriminating features in the set), and this row does not change that — it is the honest record of what NHS states for this condition specifically.

source_quote: hair thinning or hair loss
note:
IMPORTANT OVERLAP. This feature is strong support for PCOS, where the source ties it to androgen excess. Here it is weak — listed among "other symptoms" without emphasis.
That asymmetry is exactly what should happen: thinning hair raises PCOS much more than perimenopause, and age then separates them. It is the clearest example in the knowledge base of the same finding meaning different things at different ages.

source_quote: You may get more UTIs (urinary tract infections) or symptoms that feel like a UTI. This includes feeling pain or a burning sensation when you pee and needing to pee more often than usual, including at night.
note:
Same sentence, second cell — "needing to pee more often than usual, including at night" maps to the frequency value. Same overlap reasoning as pain_opening_bowels_or_urinating above.
NOTE: this is a DIFFERENT sentence from the existing urinary_symptoms= incontinence row (batch_07), which cites the separate "Other symptoms" bullet "not being able to control when you pee (urinary incontinence)". Frequency and incontinence are both genuinely stated as perimenopause symptoms by NHS, on two different parts of the same page, so both rows stand.

source_quote: feeling the need to pee more or not being able to control when you pee (urinary incontinence)
note: First and only row using the incontinence value, which was added when the feature gained it. Weak: listed under "other symptoms".

source_quote: You may get symptoms such as dryness, a burning feeling, irritation or itching in and around the vagina. These symptoms can also make sex feel painful.
note:
Weak: listed among several vaginal-dryness-related symptoms without being singled out as characteristic, and the source itself frames it as caused by falling oestrogen rather than as a defining sign.
OVERLAPS thrush's existing vulval_itching=yes row (batch_10, strong_support) — this is a real ambiguity worth flagging rather than hiding: a perimenopausal woman reporting itching is genuinely compatible with both thrush and hormonal vaginal dryness, and age_band is what should carry most of the separating weight here, not this feature. Kept weak specifically so it does not compete with thrush's strong row for a symptom thrush's own source calls "the most common symptom" of.

source_quote: Weight gain during perimenopause and menopause is common.
note: Weak because "common" describes prevalence, not a characteristic or defining sign — the same distinction that keeps age_band's own row strong while this one is not. weight_change=gain currently only supports pcos (weak_support, batch_03); this is a real and useful overlap to make explicit, since weight_change is high-burden (3) and currently does very little discriminating work with only one condition behind it. age_band remains the feature that actually separates PCOS from perimenopause, per CLAUDE.md and the condition note in conditions.yaml — this row does not change that division, it just completes the picture NHS actually states.

source_quote: Primary ovarian insufficiency (POI) happens when your ovaries stop working normally before you are 40.
note: Second of three. See under_20 above for the encoding decision. This band and 30_to_39 below cite the shorter, plainer definitional sentence rather than the teenage-years one, since neither age range is singled out the way "teenage years" is.

source_quote: Primary ovarian insufficiency (POI) happens when your ovaries stop working normally before you are 40.
note: Third of three. See under_20 above. NOTE: womenshealth's corroborating age-risk sentence — "Age. You can get POI when you're young, but it becomes more common between the ages of 35 and 40" — could arguably make 30_to_39 the strongest of the three bands rather than equal to the other two. Left equal (weak) here for consistency with the encoding decision made for adenomyosis; flagged for the reviewer to reconsider if a graded reading is preferred.

source_quote: As you get older, fertility naturally decreases. This usually starts around age 40 or later. Menstrual periods may also become irregular as you transition to menopause. If you have POI, these changes happen earlier, before age 40. Sometimes POI can start as early as the teenage years.
note:
First of three identical-strength age rows for the open "before 40" threshold — see 20_to_29 and 30_to_39 below. "Sometimes... as early as the teenage years" is the specific clause justifying under_20 separately from the other two bands, which rest on "before age 40" alone.
Weak, not strong: this is a diagnostic criterion (the defining age threshold) rather than a symptom a source calls characteristic — the same reasoning that made adenomyosis's age rows weak rather than strong.

source_quote: The first sign of POI is usually irregular or missed periods.
note: Strong: the source explicitly calls this "the first sign... usually" — the same "usually the first sign" framing that made NHS's equivalent perimenopause sentence strong_support (batch_07). Two conditions in this knowledge base now share that exact framing from their respective sources, which is expected — POI IS early perimenopause by another name, per womenshealth's own framing, whichever side of the terminology conflict is taken.

source_quote: You may see a health care provider because of difficulty getting pregnant or trouble with infertility.
note: Weak, consistent with every difficulty_conceiving row already in the grid (endometriosis, ovarian_cyst, pcos, sexually_transmitted_infection, pelvic_inflammatory_disease, hypothyroidism — all weak_support, see batch_17's note on this feature never carrying strong_support anywhere). Corroborated by womenshealth: "Women who have gone through early or premature menopause cannot get pregnant using their own eggs" — a stronger-sounding claim, but specific to the harder "premature menopause" reading MedlinePlus's own definition explicitly distinguishes POI from (see the conflict note in conditions.yaml). Kept weak and cited to MedlinePlus's own POI-specific sentence rather than womenshealth's stronger one, to avoid importing a claim that may not apply to POI under MedlinePlus's own definition of the term.

source_quote: You know you have gone through menopause when you have not had your period for 12 months in a row.
note: Mapped to over_6_months, the widest available band, rather than inventing a 12_months value the feature does not have — periods_stopped _duration's allowed_values are [not_stopped, under_3_months, 3_to_6_months, over_6_months], so 12 months in a row necessarily falls in the top band without needing a finer distinction the schema does not offer. Weak because this defines menopause generally (the same sentence NHS uses almost verbatim for perimenopause), not POI specifically — POI is distinguished from ordinary menopause by age, which the age_band rows above carry, not by this feature.

source_quote: an unusual discharge from your vagina, penis or anus
note: Listed first among STI symptoms. Strong, and it gives abnormal_discharge something to point at besides PID — which matters, because STI is the usual CAUSE of PID rather than an alternative to it.

source_quote: Problems getting pregnant or permanent infertility
note: Weak, and note what the source is actually saying: this is listed under what untreated STIs can LEAD TO, not among presenting symptoms. It is a complication, so it raises the condition only faintly.

source_quote: If the infection spreads, you might get lower abdominal (belly) pain, pain during sex, nausea, and fever.
note: Same sentence, third cell. Weak for the same reason as above.

source_quote: If the infection spreads, you might get lower abdominal (belly) pain, pain during sex, nausea, and fever.
note: Same sentence, fourth and last cell. Weak for the same reason as above. Also already pelvic_inflammatory_disease's strongest single feature (batch_05, strong_support) — here it is weak because, unlike the PID row, this source names it only as a late-stage complication rather than naming it "among the signs" the way womenshealth does for PID.

source_quote: A burning sensation when urinating
note:
Listed as one of only two symptoms in women, which is what makes it strong on a page that otherwise stresses how often chlamydia is silent. Corroborated by CDC ("burning when peeing").
Note it pulls the same way as urinary_tract_infection, which is correct and clinically real — the Office on Women's Health says STI symptoms "may be mistaken for something else, such as a urinary tract infection".

source_quote: If the infection spreads, you might get lower abdominal (belly) pain, pain during sex, nausea, and fever.
note: Same sentence, second cell. Weak for the same reason as pelvic_pain_severity above — a progression symptom, not a presenting one. This feature already supports endometriosis, fibroids, PID and thrush (see batch_10's note on it becoming one of the least discriminating features in the set); this row does not change that picture, it is simply the honest record of what the source states.

source_quote: If the infection spreads, you might get lower abdominal (belly) pain, pain during sex, nausea, and fever.
note:
Mapped to "mild" rather than "moderate" or "severe": the source names pain without grading it, and mild is the least committal reading available on our ordinal scale — the same caution CLAUDE.md asks for when a source states a finding without a threshold. Weak because this is explicitly a progression symptom ("if the infection spreads"), not a presenting one — this condition can be, and usually is, silent.
Overlaps pelvic_inflammatory_disease's own pelvic_pain_severity=severe row (batch_05), which is expected rather than a duplication error: PID is what an untreated STI progresses into, and the condition note in conditions.yaml already states this directly ("it is the CAUSE of pelvic inflammatory disease"). The two conditions sharing this feature is the grid correctly representing that causal relationship, not redundancy.

source_quote: white vaginal discharge (often like cottage cheese), which does not usually smell
note: Listed first. The descriptive detail — "like cottage cheese", "does not usually smell" — is exactly what our boolean feature throws away. A user can tell these apart; the current schema cannot. Worth revisiting if discharge conditions matter more later.

source_quote: A thick, white vaginal discharge that looks like cottage cheese and does not have a bad smell
note: Same paragraph as the thrush discharge_smell row, resting here on "A thick, white vaginal discharge that looks like cottage cheese". Strong because "thick", "white" and the cottage-cheese comparison are all stated outright rather than inferred. NHS gives the same comparison: "white vaginal discharge (often like cottage cheese), which does not usually smell".

source_quote: A thick, white vaginal discharge that looks like cottage cheese and does not have a bad smell
note: Strong because the absence of smell is written into the description of the discharge itself rather than listed separately. NHS states the same within its own discharge bullet: "white vaginal discharge (often like cottage cheese), which does not usually smell".

source_quote: soreness and stinging during sex or when you pee
note: NHS-only. womenshealth's nearest sentence is "Burning, redness, and swelling of the vagina and the vulva", which names the vagina and vulva rather than passing urine, so it is not quoted for this row. Weak because the sentence is one of three items in NHS's "Symptoms of thrush in women" list and is not singled out as characteristic. The source says nothing about what else this finding may indicate, so neither does this note.

source_quote: soreness and stinging during sex or when you pee
note: Weak. This feature now supports endometriosis, fibroids, PID and thrush — it has become one of the least discriminating in the set, which is a long way from how it was first described.

source_quote: The most common symptom of a vaginal yeast infection is extreme itchiness in and around the vagina.
note:
THE ROW THAT MAKES THRUSH IDENTIFIABLE. The source calls it THE most common symptom, which is characteristic framing rather than a list entry.
Since abnormal_discharge is a yes/no and cannot tell cottage-cheese discharge from fishy discharge, itching is the only feature that separates thrush from bacterial vaginosis. Corroborated by NHS: "itching and irritation around the vulva and vagina".

source_quote: Pressure in your lower abdomen
note: Weak. Pressure now supports fibroids, ovarian cyst and UTI, so it has become one of the less discriminating features — worth knowing when reading the grid.

source_quote: Blood in the urine. This is more common in younger women. If you see blood in your urine, tell a doctor or nurse right away.
note: First evidence row for this feature, which until now existed only to key a red-flag clause. Weak because the source names it as a symptom without emphasis; NHS lists it under urgent advice rather than among the ordinary symptoms, which is a stronger claim about urgency than about diagnosis.

source_quote: Feeling tired, shaky, confused, or weak.
note:
A genuinely new cell — none of the existing 6 rows touch tiredness. Corroborated by MedlinePlus, which separately lists "Fever, tiredness, or shakiness" among UTI symptoms in its own Summary section — two independent sources naming fatigue is why this clears the bar for a row at all, given how easily tiredness could be a symptom of almost anything.
Weak, not strong: womenshealth's own sentence bundles it with "shaky, confused, or weak" as one item rather than singling it out, and both sources list it alongside several other symptoms without calling it characteristic.
OVERLAPS anaemia_symptoms and extreme_tiredness's own note in features.yaml, which already flags that extreme_tiredness and anaemia_symptoms are correlated and can be double-counted by a user answering yes to both. Not a new problem introduced by this row — just worth remembering when reading UTI's plausibility alongside a heavy- bleeding case.

source_quote: Having a fever, which may mean the infection has reached your kidneys
note: Weak, and deliberately below the PID fever row, which is strong. The source frames fever as a sign the infection has SPREAD rather than as a sign of a UTI itself. Fever now supports both conditions and remains one of the few features that separates infection from the phase 1 three.

source_quote: lower tummy pain or pain in your back, just under the ribs
note: Weak, and the mapping is partial: the source names two sites and our feature covers one. The same sentence appears in the NHS urgent-advice box, where it signals possible kidney infection — so back pain with a UTI is a more serious finding than this weak row conveys. The urgency belongs in a red flag, not in the weight.

source_quote: pain or a burning sensation when peeing (dysuria)
note:
Listed first among UTI symptoms and corroborated by the Office on Women's Health ("Pain or burning when urinating"). Strong.
Note this feature covers bowels AND urination in one question, so a yes answer does not distinguish which. That imprecision now matters more than it did, because endometriosis claims the same feature for cyclical bowel and bladder pain. Splitting the feature is worth considering.

source_quote: needing to pee more often than usual
note: This is the row that stops urinary frequency pointing at fibroids by default. Both conditions claim it, but a UTI is far commoner, and a differential that omits the common explanation systematically over-suspects the rare one.

source_quote: Feeling “full” in the lower abdomen (belly)—this is sometimes called pelvic pressure
note: A bulk effect, and the most discriminating fibroid feature: neither PCOS nor endometriosis is characterised by a sensation of fullness or pressure. Corroborated by the Office on Women's Health, which lists both "Feeling of fullness in the pelvic area" and "Enlargement of the lower abdomen".

source_quote: Age. Fibroids become more common as women age, especially during the 30s and 40s through menopause. After menopause, fibroids usually shrink.
note: A risk factor, not a presenting sign, so weak. Age is cheap to ask (burden 1) and shifts several conditions at once, which is why it earns its place despite being weak individually.

source_quote: Age. Fibroids become more common as women age, especially during the 30s and 40s through menopause. After menopause, fibroids usually shrink.
Fibroids mainly affect women who have not been through the menopause.
note:
THE ELIMINATION ROW for fibroids, and the NHS states it far more directly than any other source — it is a statement about who the condition affects, not an inference from a symptom being absent, which the protocol forbids. The same page lists "have not reached the menopause" among the causes, and the Office on Women's Health corroborates: "After menopause, fibroids usually shrink."
This is the ONLY elimination lever fibroids have. Because "Fibroids do not always cause symptoms", the absence of any given symptom argues against fibroids far less than it would for a condition that is always symptomatic. MAPPING CAVEAT: 55_plus is a proxy for post-menopausal, and some women reach menopause earlier — the row will miss them.

source_quote: Anemia (when you don’t have enough red blood cells)
note: Named directly as a symptom of fibroids, and the Office on Women's Health ties it explicitly to the bleeding: "Heavy bleeding (which can be heavy enough to cause anemia)". This is what turns heavy bleeding from a description into a question about whether it is having an effect.

source_quote: Heavy or painful periods or bleeding between periods
note: Same sentence as the row above, which is legitimate — one source sentence supports two cells. Weak rather than strong because bleeding between periods appears last in a list of alternatives rather than being emphasised.

source_quote: Heavy or painful periods or bleeding between periods
note: First symptom listed, and corroborated by NICHD ("Heavy bleeding or painful periods") and by the NHS heavy periods page, which names fibroids among the causes.

source_quote: Reproductive problems, such as infertility, multiple miscarriages, and early onset of labor during pregnancy
note: Weak, and deliberately so: the Office on Women's Health calls fibroid infertility "very rare". Infertility also appears under PCOS and endometriosis, so it separates the differential very little.

source_quote: pain or discomfort during sex
note:
ADDED TO CORRECT AN ERROR. Batch 02 asserted that pain during sex distinguished endometriosis because "neither PCOS nor fibroids is characterised by it". The NHS fibroids page lists it plainly among fibroid symptoms, so that was wrong and the grid has to say so.
Weak rather than strong: the NHS lists it without emphasis and the page says "Fibroids do not always cause symptoms", whereas the Office on Women's Health frames it as characteristic for endometriosis. The feature still separates the two, but by degree rather than absolutely.

source_quote: Frequent urination (caused by a fibroid pressing on the bladder)
note: The source states the mechanism, not just the association — a fibroid pressing on the bladder — which is characteristic framing rather than a bare list entry. Note this is FREQUENCY, not difficulty passing urine; difficulty is a red flag and is handled separately.
